DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

## What the review proposes

The review proposes:
- £1 price rises on fish and chips and the burger, and £2 on the sirloin steak, all staying below the competitor midpoint for each dish;
- replacing the mushroom risotto, which it says has the weakest margin and lowest sales.

It projects £810 a week (£42,120 a year) in extra gross profit and a main-course margin of about 71%.

## Verdict

The price rises themselves are reasonable. They are modest (6–8%), and all three stay below the competitor midpoint. But two parts of the case are contradicted by the paper's own figures, and the projected gain is substantially overstated:

1. **The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu (80%), not the weakest.** Replacing it at the same price with a special would probably *lose* gross profit.
2. **The £810 projection ignores the beef price rise the paper itself reports.** The rise takes effect on the same day.
3. **The gains appear to include VAT.** In the UK, menu prices include 20% VAT, so each £1 increase is about £0.83 to the business.

On corrected figures, the gain is probably nearer £10,000–£20,000 a year than £42,000, and the main-course margin stays at about 70%, not 71%.

## Arithmetic

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Margins in Table 1 | 1 − cost ÷ price | 69% / 72% / 75% / 60% / **80%** ✓ |
| Weekly gain | £310 + £260 + (£2 × 120) | £810 ✓ |
| Annual gain | £810 × 52 | £42,120 ✓ |
| Competitor midpoints | £17.98 / £16.50 / £29.50 | All three new prices below ✓ |
| Margin after rises | Named dishes, excluding specials | About 71% ✓, but only before beef costs rise |
| Trading days | Wednesday to Sunday | **Five, not six** (§8) ✗ |

## 1. The risotto is the most profitable dish by margin

Table 1 gives the risotto an 80% margin, the highest on the menu. "Weakest margin" is the opposite of what the table shows, and the author's note repeats it.

In cash terms the risotto makes £11.20 a plate. That's more than the burger (£10.80) and the curry (£10.90), and close to fish and chips (£11.40). Its sales of 90 plates a week are tied with specials for lowest.

The replacement is likely to earn less. Specials currently run at a 64% margin. A special at £14.00 and 64% margin makes about £8.96 a plate, roughly **£2.24 less than the risotto**. At 90 plates a week, that's about £200 a week (£10,000 a year) of lost gross profit.

If the risotto's low sales are the concern, there are better options: reposition it on the menu, or rotate a seasonal *risotto*, which keeps its low food cost.

## 2. The beef price rise is left out

§4 reports a 12% rise in beef prices from 1 April, the same day the new menu prices take effect. §5.3 assumes food costs don't change.

Upper-bound cost increase, treating each plate's whole food cost as beef:

| Dish | Extra cost per plate | Plates a week | Extra cost a week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £0.50 | 260 | about £130 |
| Steak | £1.25 | 120 | about £150 |
| **Total** | | | **about £280** |

The true figure is a little lower, because buns, chips and sides aren't beef. But most of the steak's cost is beef. On this basis:
- the steak's net gain from its £2 rise is under £1 a plate;
- the main-course margin comes out at about 70%, not 71%.

## 3. The figures appear to include VAT

UK menu prices must include VAT, so a £1 menu increase brings in about £0.83 of net revenue. On that basis, the £810 becomes about **£675 a week**. Food cost is not subject to this, so the margins in Table 1 are also overstated if they are calculated on menu prices including VAT. Fish and chips, for example, is about 63% on its net price of £13.75, not 69%.

Check how your accounts calculate gross profit. If the 70% target is measured net of VAT, as is usual, every margin figure in the paper needs restating on the same basis.

## Corrected weekly projection

| Item | Per week |
|---|---|
| Price increases, net of VAT | +£675 |
| Beef cost rise (upper bound) | −£280 |
| Risotto replaced by a 64%-margin special | −£200 |
| **Net change** | **about +£195 (about £10,000 a year)** |

If the risotto stays, the gain is about £395 a week, roughly £20,000 a year. Either figure is still positive and worth having, but it is a long way from £42,000.

## 4. Volumes and monitoring

- **Loyalty doesn't mean customers won't react to prices.** Repeat customers (60% of bookings) are also the ones most likely to notice price rises. The modest size of the increases is a better reason to expect volumes to hold than the repeat-booking figure.
- **The monitoring compares different seasons.** January and February are usually quiet, and April and May are typically busier, so a rise in plates sold could hide lost demand from the price rises. Comparing with the same weeks last year would show the effect more clearly.
- **Set a trigger in advance.** Decide now what fall in plates sold of a dish would lead you to review its price.

## What holds

These parts of the review are sound:
- The Table 1 margin arithmetic, on the paper's own basis.
- The competitor comparison: all three new prices sit below the midpoint, and the increases are modest.
- The case for raising prices at all, given the margin falling from 70% to 67% and no price change since September 2024.
- Not raising the curry price. It is already the dish with the second-highest margin, and there is no competitor data for it.
- Weekly monitoring by dish.

## Summary

**Settled now:**
- The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the lowest.
- The projection leaves out the beef price rise, which reduces the gain by up to about £280 a week.
- The gains appear to include VAT.
- The restaurant trades five days a week, not six.

**Still open, and what would settle each:**

| Question | How to settle it |
|---|---|
| Whether margins are measured before or after VAT | Check against how your accounts calculate gross profit |
| The exact effect of the beef rise | Separate the beef content of the burger and steak plate costs |
| Whether volumes hold | Weekly monitoring against the same weeks last year |

**Recommendation:** approve the three price rises. Keep the mushroom risotto, or replace it with a dish that matches its food cost. Before the owners rely on the projection, restate it net of VAT and after the beef price rise.
